title: Chapter 9: A Very Tidy Cause
blurb: Ravi names the firm behind the cracked east stair and sends the proof across the city by courier, but a midnight ruling can hand the weight straight back.

blocks.text: I signed for the east stair at ten past seven on the morning of day twenty-nine, because by then I knew what it stood on. It had taken me two days and most of two nights to find out. This time the pen went across the TAKEN BY line like any pen on any paper, and the book took my name, and the stair came down into my legs.
WO-1-001 FLOOR 1. PUBLIC FLOOR. TIER 1. FAULT: CRACK. EAST STAIR, FOOTING TO FLOOR 4. CAUSE: UNDIAGNOSED. GRADE REQUIRED: 1. SYMPTOM: LOAD, CARRIED IN THE LEGS. STATUS: TAKEN. TAKEN BY: R. ANAND.

I'd pictured the ache after a long day up a ladder. It was the stair. Every tread and landing and the brick wall it climbs, four storeys of it, settling down through my hips into my knees as if someone had lowered it onto me off a crane and let the chain go slack. I was sitting down when it arrived, which was the one sensible thing I did all morning. My knees made a noise I'd only ever heard from old floorboards.
Dusty lifted his head off his paws on the office mat, looked at me, put it down again, and sighed.
"I know," I said. "He told me to wait till I knew. I waited."

The fever from floor 6 was still in my face, and the burns on my knuckles had gone shiny and tight. I sat with my hands flat on the green cloth and let the weight find where it was going to live, and went over the two days again, because I was about to put a name to it, and I don't put my name to a cause I haven't seen.

The first day I'd spent underneath it, in the crawlway off the boiler room, on my elbows with a torch in my teeth, and found what Nessa had told me I'd find. Holes in the footing a hand apart, clean and round, cored right through the old lime, and the brick between them opened from hole to hole like paper torn along its dotted line. That was a stair that had been drilled. But a stair that loses its footing drops at the bottom. It doesn't split to the fourth floor in an afternoon, not a stair built in 1925 by people who used more brick than they needed.
So something else had been holding it, and that had gone as well.

I found the something else that night on the fourth-floor landing, with my head tipped back. In the plaster under the top flight there were four round bumps in a row, painted over so many times they'd gone soft at the edges. I scraped one with my thumbnail and found iron. The end of a rod, threaded, with a nut on it. The top of the east stair wasn't sitting on anything. It was hanging.
The drawings behind the office door don't show any rods. They show four storeys and a roof and a stair that stands on its own feet. But a hanger has to hang from something, so I went up to find what.

They went to floor 6. On floor 5 they ran inside the east wall; with my ear to the wallpaper I could hear them ring when the lift moved. On floor 6 they came up through the boiler-hall floor behind the iron gantry, rods as thick as my thumb, and each one was held on top of a riveted beam by a brass collar nut the size of a teacup.
Most of the collars were bright. One had split down its side, and its rod had slipped through it the width of a finger.

I'd put my hand on the split collar, then on a bright one, then taken the stamped jumper I'd pulled off the hot run out of my trouser pocket and held it in my other hand. They all said GRADE 2 in the same neat stamp. In my hands they all felt the same: new brass, plain grade one, nothing in them.
"I FITTED WHAT CAME," the furnace lodger had said through the vents when I asked. It hadn't sounded sorry. It sounded hungry. "THE PAPER SAID WHERE."
The paper was in the Greyfold box I'd kept, the one Kit had brought, under the tissue where I hadn't looked. A packing note, typed.
JUMPERS: HOT RUN. COLLARS: EAST HANGERS, BEAM 2. FIT ON RECEIPT.
So that was what the stair stood on. A footing at the bottom and iron at the top, and somebody had drilled the one and dressed the other in brass that couldn't hold it.
I uncapped the pen and put the nib on the CAUSE line, and the first thing I meant to write was the lodger.
It had fitted them. It had told me so itself. Nobody had pushed it or flooded it out or chased it off its nest. It had been offered coal and said yes, the way I say yes to soup. That's a cause.
The nib was touching the paper. I could feel the weight in my knees pushing up into the seat.
Then I thought about the key-eaters.

I'd put an order on them in my first week with the book, because they'd bitten the riser's joints and I'd seen the bites. They disputed anyway. They said the white had come and put them out of their old nest, and at midnight the building agreed with them, because the reason underneath beats the reason on top. The order came back to me and I carried it doubled for days, because I'd stopped at the first party I could see.

The lodger wasn't the key-eaters. It hadn't been driven. But it hadn't chosen what was in the box either, or where the box said to put it. Somebody had typed BEAM 2. Somebody had stamped GRADE 2 on brass that wasn't, and sent it to the one occupant who would fit anything for coal. If I served the lodger, the lodger would dispute with that packing note, and the note would be the better evidence, and the order would come home to me with a day gone. I didn't have a day to spare.
And behind Greyfold there was nobody. Nobody had made them drill, or buy soft brass and pay a furnace to fit it. Two jobs on one stair, by one firm that chose both.
"It's them," I told Dusty. "Isn't it."
Dusty didn't say anything, because in the basement he's a dog. But he came and put his chin on my knee, which hurt a great deal, and I let him.

I wrote it out on the back of an envelope first and read it twice. Then I wrote it in the book in my own square capitals, which look worse every time next to the copperplate. I wrote the party underneath. And then the book, in the hand that isn't mine and isn't Walter's, added a line I hadn't written.

WO-1-001 CAUSE: EAST STAIR FOOTING CORED. EAST HANGERS FITTED WITH UNDER-GRADE COLLARS, SUPPLIED AND DIRECTED. ONE PARTY. PARTY: GREYFOLD PROPERTY PARTNERS (WRECKING PERMIT). OFFICER OF RECORD: I. TARRANT. TAKEN BY: R. ANAND. STATUS: TAKEN.
It didn't bounce. I read the officer line twice, lips moving, and thought about the woman who'd told me to be nice to a mould.

Then I tore the carbon slip off along its perforations, folded it once, put it in an envelope, and wrote on the front: I. TARRANT, GREYFOLD PROPERTY PARTNERS. INTO HER HAND. FROM R. ANAND, PELLORY COURT.
Then I tried to stand up.

It took two goes and the edge of the desk. Walking was the stair walking, the whole height of it coming down through one knee and then the other. The basement steps were out of the question, so I took the service lift up one floor like a man of ninety, with Dusty.
The doors shut. The car lifted, the floor came up under me, and both my knees went off like cap guns.
"Sorry," I said to them. "Sorry, that's me, I know. You never asked for a stair."
Then I talked to the stair instead, since it was in there with us.
"Listen," I said. "By tonight it won't be my legs carrying you. You'll be on the people who drilled you. That's a promise. Tonight."
Dusty looked at the doors.
"I know," I said. "Six o'clock tomorrow. I've read the letter."

I couldn't take it to Greyfold myself. Their office was a glass front on Chandler Row, the far side of the city. On these legs it would have taken half the day and a lie to get past their desk, with no caretaker left behind me. But Walter had told me, on floor 5, the night the key-eaters won, that a slip a courier carries counts as served by whoever sent it. And I knew a courier who had never had a door they couldn't find.

I didn't have Kit's number. I had the Errandry app and the tip tin, which was also the coal money. I booked a listed run, Pellory Court to Greyfold Property Partners, Chandler Row, one envelope, recipient signature only. In the box marked Notes for your rider I typed: For Kit, if Kit's on. It's the building with the floors.
Then I sat on the bottom step of the east stair, above the crack, and waited.
Nessa came down at ten, on the edges, with a bowl of dumpling broth, and looked at the way I was sitting.
"You took it," she said.
"This morning."
"Good. Eat." She watched me lift the spoon. "On who?"
"Greyfold."
She thought about that like she was checking a weld. "Yes," she said. "Who carries it?"
"A courier. If the courier comes."
"I will write that you sat on a step all day, Mr Caretaker," she said. "It is true." She went back up on the edges, coughing her dry cough on the turn, and I ate all of it.
Kit came at ten to one, helmet still on, phone in hand, and stood in the doorway looking at me on the step.
"Building with the floors," Kit said. "That's what it says. You wrote that."
"I wrote that."
"Twice you gave me lift timings. Weight limits. Five stars on the weight, one on you." Kit came in. "So say it. I'm not taking anything anywhere till you say it properly."

I could have handed Kit an envelope, said it was urgent and told them nothing, and Kit would have done it, because Kit never asks what's in the box. Everybody in this city had been doing that to Kit for eleven months.

"There are floors," I said. "Above the fourth. I can get to two of them. The boxes you bring go to whoever lives up there, and some of what's in them is made to break. A stair cracked because of it. That stair." I pointed at the crack under my feet. "And what's in this envelope says the firm that did it has to carry it, instead of me. It has to go into one woman's hand. Not the desk. Hers."
Kit looked at the crack, then at the lift doors down the back corridor, then at me.
"Okay," they said, quieter. "Okay. Five stars for that." They held out a hand. "Who's the woman?"
"Imogen Tarrant. She'll come down if the desk says Pellory Court."

Kit put the envelope inside their jacket, flat against their chest, and zipped it. "Every one of those furnace boxes," they said, "was a Greyfold pickup. Same depot, same tape. It's all on my run history."
"Keep that. Don't delete any of it."
"I never delete anything." Kit was already at the door. "I'll ring you from the road. Put me on speaker. You'll want the route."
"Thank you," I said, and then again, and Kit said every thank-you after the first was costing me a star.
They rang before they'd reached the bins. I put them on speaker on the step beside me, and for forty minutes the east stair got the whole of Vellhaven in Kit's voice.

"Out of Wickline, left at the bins, through the car park behind the launderette, under the sign that says no cycling, cycling. Hill. Hill's three stars, it's got a view. Right on Ferry Road. Bus lane's mine." Wind roared down the phone. "Over the old bridge, left at the lights nobody waits at, and that's Chandler Row. Glass. One star for glass, you can't lock a bike to glass."

I talked back, to the phone and to the stair. I told the stair it was nearly there. The weight hadn't eased at all. When a lorry went by outside, the whole flight seemed to settle a finger lower onto me, and my hands went white on my thighs, and my face burned with the fever on top of it.

"Going in," Kit said. "Desk. Lady on the desk, four stars, very shiny. Hello. Delivery for I. Tarrant, recipient signature only. From Pellory Court." A pause, and a handset lifted somewhere further off. "She's ringing up. She said Pellory Court twice. Okay. Lifts. Lift's opening."
I heard heels on stone, coming closer and slowing down.
"Hello," said Imogen Tarrant, a little way from the phone. Warm and quick. "You're not one of ours."
"Errandry," Kit said. "Into your hand, it says. Not the desk."
"Into my hand." A small laugh. "All right, then."
Paper. I put my palm flat on the tread beside the crack.
And the stair went.

It didn't go gradually either. It lifted off me the way a load lifts when the crane takes it back, all at once and from the top, and my knees came up so fast I nearly stood without meaning to. The fever was still in my face. My knuckles still stung. But my legs were my own legs again, and the tread under my hand was only a cold tread.
"That's you off me," I told it. "I said tonight. It's not even two o'clock."
On the phone something soft and heavy happened, like a bag of shopping being set down.

"Oh," Kit said. Then, in a voice I hadn't heard from them before, careful and flat, the way people read aloud in church: "Ravi. She has sat down. On the floor of her lobby. Not on a chair. The lady from the desk is coming round." A pause. "I would like you to tell me what I just gave her."
"The stair," I said. "The weight of it. It's hers till her people fix it."
"Is she going to be all right?"
"Her legs'll be heavy. She'll be able to stand, slowly. It's what I had this morning."
There was a rustle, and then Imogen was on the line herself, close and low. Her sentences had got shorter.
"Ravi."
"Hello, Imogen."
"That's a very tidy cause." I heard her breathe out through her teeth. "Two jobs, one stair. Clever."
"It's true," I said.
"Most things are, partly." Quieter still: "I'll be disputing. You'd do the same. Look at your board tonight." And then, kinder, which was worse: "Tell your courier they did very well."

The phone went back to Kit, who said, still formal, "I am leaving the building now," and then, out in the wind, in their own voice: "She looked at me like a parcel she never ordered. One star. Ravi, what even was that?"
"I'll tell you all of it," I said. "Come back by. There's usually soup."

By evening I could walk the east stair like anyone, on the edges, and I did, all the way up and down, because I could. In the office the floor 1 page said STATUS: TRANSFERRED, and the header had gone light again.
CARETAKER: R. ANAND GRADE: 1 (ODD-JOB) CREDITS: 11 HOLDING: 1 CERTIFIED: 5
Holding one. The hot run's fever, and nothing in my legs.

At about nine the lobby board changed. It's cork in a frame beside the post table, and it carries Mrs Quarry's association minutes and a lost-cat notice from 2A. Next to the cat, pinned with nobody's pin, there was now the third carbon of WO-1-001, and beside it a second sheet in a quick, neat hand I knew from the business card in my wallet.

DISPUTE. WO-1-001. FILED BY: GREYFOLD PROPERTY PARTNERS. OFFICER OF RECORD: I. TARRANT. The footing was cored under the permit, as a licensed site investigation. The collars were fitted by the occupant of floor 6, which chose to fit them and was paid to. The nearer cause is the occupant.
Under both, in copperplate: RULING AT MIDNIGHT.

It was the cause I'd nearly written that morning. I read it twice and agreed with every word except the last sentence. The permit didn't make them drill, the same way the coal didn't make the lodger. Somebody chose, at the top, and I had the paper that said who.
Lou Mabbott came in from the bakery with Danny and a bag of broken loaves, and stopped beside me in front of the board.
"Greyfold," she said, reading. "Good. About time they paid for something." She frowned. "Floor 6? There's no floor 6, love. They've typed a 6 for a 1. Can't even spell the building."
She gave me two of the loaves and took Danny up the wall side.

I took the loaves to floor 6 at eleven, because I owed the lodger coal on Thursday and had no coal, and bread burns. Dusty came. The boiler hall was hot along the run where my fever lives, and the furnace at the far end was low and sulky.
"Greyfold says you chose," I told it. "They've put it on the board."
"I DID CHOOSE," the lodger said, through every vent at once. "COAL IS COAL."
"I know. So would I, for soup. But they chose what went in the box, and where it went. That's what I've told the building."
"WILL IT COME TO ME?"
"Not from me."

It took the bread anyway. I went behind the gantry and put my hand on the split collar on beam 2. It was still soft in my palm. The rod was still a finger low. The crack was still under the first tread, far below, with seven hours to six o'clock.
Back in the lift, Dusty sat down in the open doorway, half in the car and half on floor 6, and Walter looked up at me out of the dog's face.
"Good cause, son," he said. "Took you two days."
"I think I win," I said. "The note's better than her nearer link. Then it's done, isn't it? By the morning."
He answered the way he always does, with something to do.

"Go and read your board at midnight," Walter said. "And understand what you're reading. If you win, son, that stair stays in her legs until her people fix it. If you lose, it comes back to you, and it's still cracked at six."
